scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that discipline is central to learning, then argues schools can and do motivate; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: In the end, no one can learn a subject for us, since we must do the work ourselves.
Some people argue that learning is primarily a matter of personal discipline, and that schools or colleges alone cannot motivate students.
I agree that personal discipline is vital, but I disagree that schools play only a small part in motivating students to learn.
First, personal discipline truly is at the centre of all real learning.
Even the best school cannot help a student who refuses to study, practise, or pay attention.
For example, two students in the same class often achieve very different results because of their own effort.
This shows that the will to work hard usually matters more than any single teacher or method.
Students who take charge of their own learning keep going long after a course has ended.
Lasting knowledge depends on the steady self-discipline that only the learner can supply.
In this sense, the statement points to something genuinely important.
Second, however, it is wrong to claim that schools cannot motivate students at all.
A skilled and caring teacher can awaken interest in a subject a student once found boring.
Consider a bored pupil who suddenly loves science because an inspiring teacher made it exciting and clear.
Such cases show that good schools can spark the very motivation that personal discipline then sustains.
Encouragement, good teaching, and a positive environment all help students want to work hard.
Many students who once lacked discipline have found it after a teacher truly believed in them.
Schools and self-discipline, then, work together rather than one replacing the other.
In conclusion, personal discipline is indeed essential to genuine learning.
But schools and teachers can do a great deal to spark and support that discipline.
The best learning grows where a student's own effort meets the encouragement of a good school.
